topics.blurb: The data shapes, functions and error handling that most AI code is made of.
topics.why: Model APIs send and receive nested data. Reading and reshaping it confidently removes most early friction.

items.objective: Read and build the nested dictionaries and lists that AI APIs exchange, and wrap each reshaping step in a small function that fails clearly when data is missing.

items.objective: Handle timeouts, HTTP errors and invalid replies without hiding them.
planned: Which exceptions to catch, and which to let surface

items.title: Virtual environments and dependencies
items.objective: Keep each project's packages separate and reproducible.

items.title: Type hints and runtime validation
items.objective: Use type hints for readability and Pydantic for checks at runtime.
planned: What type hints do and do not enforce

topics.why: Every hosted model is reached through an HTTP API. Knowing the request flow makes failures readable instead of mysterious.

python-data-shapes.title: Python data shapes for AI apps: dictionaries, lists and functions
python-data-shapes.summary: Read and reshape the nested dictionaries and lists that model APIs send and receive.
python-data-shapes.objective: Read and build the nested dictionaries and lists that AI APIs exchange, and wrap each reshaping step in a small function that fails clearly when data is missing.
python-data-shapes.intro: Most code around a language model is not about the model. It moves data: building a request from saved notes, pulling text out of a response, recording what happened. In Python that data arrives as **dictionaries** and **lists**, usually nested inside each other. Getting fluent with these two shapes, and with small functions that name each step, removes a large share of the friction in AI projects.
keyIdeas: A dictionary maps keys to values; a list keeps items in order by position.
API responses nest them. Walk a nested value one bracket at a time.
A function gives one reshaping step a name, inputs and a single return value.
A missing key raises KeyError. Decide on purpose whether to fail loudly or use a default.

sections.title: Dictionaries: values found by name
sections.body:
A dictionary stores **key: value** pairs. You look a value up by its key rather than by position, which makes dictionaries the natural shape for records: a request, a response, a configuration. Keys must be immutable, so strings and numbers are typical keys; values can be anything, including other dictionaries and lists.

Three operations cover most needs: `d[key]` reads a value and raises `KeyError` if the key is absent; `d.get(key, default)` returns the default instead; and `key in d` checks without reading. Looping over `d.items()` gives you each key with its value.

sections.title: Lists: values found by position
sections.body:
A list keeps items in order. Positions start at **0**, and negative positions count from the end, so `items[-1]` is the last item. Lists grow with `append`, and a `for` loop visits each item in order.

Model APIs use lists wherever order matters: the turns of a conversation, the content blocks of a reply, a set of retrieved passages. When you see a list in a response, ask two questions: *could it be empty?* and *does the position mean anything, or should I look for the item by a field such as its type?*
sections.code:
messages = []
messages.append({"role": "user", "content": "Hello"})
messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": "Hi!"})
messages[0]["role"]   # "user"
messages[-1]["content"]  # "Hi!"
len(messages)          # 2

sections.title: Nesting: following a path
sections.body: Real responses combine the two shapes. To reach a value, read the path from the outside in: each pair of brackets is one step, a **string key** into a dictionary or an **integer position** into a list. Writing the path out loud ("the content list, its first block, that block's text") catches most mistakes before you run anything.
sections.callout: If a step fails, print the value one level up: `type(x)` and `x.keys()` or `len(x)` usually show what you have instead.

sections.title: Functions: naming one step
sections.body:
A function packages a step so it can be named, tested and reused. Parameters are its inputs; `return` hands back one value. A function that reaches its end without a `return` statement returns `None`, which is a common source of confusing errors further along.

Small functions with clear names (`build_request`, `reply_text`, `count_output_tokens`) make AI code easier to follow than one long block, and each can be checked separately with a known input. Type hints such as `-> str` document intent; Python does not enforce them at run time.

sections.title: Worked example: joining the text of a reply
sections.body:
A Messages-style reply holds a list of content blocks. Some are text; others (for example tool requests) are not. The task is to join the text blocks into one string.

1. **Start from the outside**: the reply is a dictionary; its `"content"` key holds a list.
2. **Loop over the list**, because the number of blocks varies.
3. **Choose by field, not by position**: keep blocks whose `"type"` is `"text"`.
4. **Return one value**, so the caller decides what to do with it.

Learning Desk does the same thing with the provider SDK's objects in `provider.py`: it joins `block.text` for every block whose `block.type` is `"text"`.

sections.title: Misconception: .get() is always the safer choice
sections.body:
`d.get(key)` never raises, which can feel safer. But for a value your code *needs*, it only postpones the failure: `None` flows onward and breaks later, far from the cause, often with a less helpful message.

Use square brackets for **required** fields, so a malformed record fails immediately where the problem is. Use `.get()` with an explicit default for **optional** fields, where absence is normal. When data comes from outside your program (a model, a file, a web page), validate it once at the boundary rather than sprinkling defaults throughout.

json-basics.title: JSON: the shape of data on the wire
json-basics.summary: Recognise JSON's six value types, convert to and from Python, and describe an expected shape.
json-basics.objective: Read any JSON document by identifying its value types, convert it to and from Python, and explain why successful parsing does not mean the data is what you expected.
json-basics.intro: JSON is the format most AI APIs use for both requests and responses, and the format Learning Desk uses to store model output. It is plain text with a small grammar, which is why nearly every language can read it. The skill is not memorising the grammar; it is reading a document's **shape** quickly and knowing what parsing does and does not check.
keyIdeas: JSON has four primitive types (string, number, boolean, null) and two structured types (object, array).
json.loads turns JSON text into Python objects; json.dumps turns them back into text.
Parsing checks syntax only. It does not check that the fields you need are present or sensible.
A JSON Schema states the expected shape: types, properties and which are required.

sections.title: Six kinds of value
sections.body:
An **object** is an unordered set of name–value pairs in braces; names are always strings in double quotes. An **array** is an ordered list in square brackets. Everything else is a **string** (double quotes), a **number**, `true`/`false`, or `null`.

Notice what is missing: there is no date type, no integer-versus-decimal distinction in the grammar, and no comments. Dates travel as strings by convention, which is why a schema or documentation must say which format to expect. The standard also says names within an object *should* be unique; when they are not, different software may behave differently.

sections.title: Text in, objects out
sections.body:
`json.loads` (load *string*) parses text into Python objects; `json.dumps` (dump *string*) serialises them back into text. Use `indent=2` when a person will read the result.

A parse either succeeds completely or raises an error; there is no partial result. Code that parses data from outside the program (a model reply, an import) should expect that error and report it rather than crash or guess.
sections.code:
import json

text = '{"minutes": 20, "complete": true, "tags": ["tokens"]}'
record = json.loads(text)
record["complete"]        # True (a Python bool)
record["tags"][0]         # "tokens"
json.dumps(record, indent=2)  # back to text

try:
    json.loads('{"minutes": 20,}')   # trailing comma
except json.JSONDecodeError as error:
    print("Not valid JSON:", error)

sections.title: Syntax is not meaning
sections.body:
`json.loads` tells you the text is well-formed JSON. It says nothing about whether the object has the keys you need, whether a number is in range, or whether a list is empty. All of these parse successfully:

- `{}`: a valid, empty object.
- `{"answer": null}`: the key is present but holds nothing.
- `{"minutes": "twenty"}`: the right key with the wrong type.

Checking shape and meaning is a separate step, either with explicit code or with a schema validator. Learning Desk always does that second step before saving model output.
sections.callout: Parsed is not the same as valid. Keep the two words distinct in your head and in your error messages.

sections.title: Describing shape with JSON Schema
sections.body:
JSON Schema is itself JSON. The core keywords are `type` (what kind of value), `properties` (the expected keys of an object and a schema for each) and `required` (keys that must be present). A schema is useful twice: as documentation a person can read, and as input to a validator or a model provider that can enforce it.

Learning Desk generates schemas from Pydantic models and sends them with structured-output requests; the *Structured outputs* lesson follows that path in detail.

sections.title: Worked example: checking a saved record
sections.body: Suppose a quiz question arrives as JSON text. Parsing is step one; then check the fields you rely on and one rule a basic schema cannot express: the answer must be one of the options. Learning Desk applies that same rule to generated multiple-choice questions before saving them.
sections.code:
import json

raw = '{"question": "What is a token?", "options": ["A word", "A piece of text"], ' \
      '"answer": "A piece of text"}'
record = json.loads(raw)

missing = [k for k in ("question", "options", "answer") if k not in record]
if missing:
    raise ValueError(f"Missing fields: {missing}")
if not isinstance(record["options"], list):
    raise ValueError("options must be a list")
if record["answer"] not in record["options"]:
    raise ValueError("answer must be one of the options")

sections.title: Misconception: valid JSON means correct data
sections.body:
A reply that parses is only *readable*. It can still be missing fields, have values of the wrong type, contain an answer that is not among the options, or be factually wrong. Each of those needs its own check, and the last one (truth) usually cannot be checked by code at all.

A useful habit is to name each check explicitly in error messages: "not JSON", "missing field", "wrong type", "rule broken". When something fails later, you will know which layer to look at.

http-request-flow.title: HTTP and API calls: following one request
http-request-flow.summary: Trace a model call from click to storage, read requests and responses, and plan for failure.
http-request-flow.objective: Trace an API call from the interface to storage, name the parts of an HTTP request and response, and decide in advance what should happen at each kind of failure.
http-request-flow.intro: When you press a button that "asks the AI", a chain of ordinary software runs: your interface, a backend, an HTTPS request across the internet, a provider's servers, and code that checks and stores the result. Each link can fail independently. Seeing the whole chain turns error messages into locations you can reason about.
keyIdeas: HTTP is request and response: method, path, headers and body go out; status, headers and body come back.
Status classes: 2xx success, 4xx a problem with the request, 5xx a problem on the server side.
HTTP is stateless: each request stands alone unless the client sends context again.
Every step can fail. Decide what is recorded and shown before it happens.

sections.title: Request and response
sections.body:
A request has a **method** (what to do, such as GET to read or POST to submit), a **path** (which resource), **headers** (metadata such as content type and credentials) and, for POST, a **body** with the data. The response mirrors it: a **status code** with a short reason, headers, and a body.

Model APIs typically use POST with a JSON body describing the model, limits and messages. The JSON reply contains the generated content, a stop reason and token usage.

sections.body: Read the status before the body. A 2xx body is a result; a 4xx or 5xx body is an error description. The first digit tells you who should act: 4xx means something about *your* request needs to change; 5xx means the server had a problem, and the same request might succeed later.

sections.title: Following a request through Learning Desk
sections.body:
In this app, `provider.build_request` assembles the request (model, token limit, instructions, one user message, and an output schema). `provider.send` makes **exactly one attempt**: the SDK client is created with `max_retries=0`, and each known failure (401, 403, 404, 429, 400, other statuses, timeouts, connection errors) becomes a readable message.

`ai._run` times the call, parses and validates the reply, and inserts an `ai_calls` record **whether the call succeeded or failed**, including the request sent, the raw response, the model reported back, token usage and elapsed time. That record is what *Inspect AI call* shows.

sections.title: Retries and idempotency
sections.body:
A request is **idempotent** if sending it twice has the same effect as sending it once. GET is designed to be; POST is not guaranteed to be. A model call is a POST, and every attempt is processed and billed separately, so a retry is a decision, not a free action.

Anthropic's SDK retries some transient failures (connection errors, rate limits, 5xx) automatically, twice by default. Learning Desk turns that off so one click is at most one billable attempt, and asks you to retry deliberately. Other applications reasonably choose automatic retries with backoff; what matters is choosing on purpose.
sections.callout: Before adding automatic retries to a billed call, decide the maximum number of attempts and what the user sees while they happen.

sections.title: Worked example: reading one failure
sections.body:
Suppose you click **Generate quick read** during a burst of activity and the provider answers 429. Follow it through the code:

1. The SDK raises `RateLimitError`; `provider.send` converts it to "Rate limited (429). Wait and try again." with the provider's details.
2. `ai._run` catches the error, records `status='error'`, the message, and the elapsed time.
3. Nothing is saved as a summary, so the reader still offers the button.
4. You can open the call record to see exactly what was sent and what came back.

No retry happened, nothing was invented, and the failure is inspectable later.

sections.title: Misconception: a 200 response means the answer is right
sections.body:
200 means the server processed the request. The content can still be unusable: the reply may have stopped at the token limit (`stop_reason` of `max_tokens`) and be incomplete, the model may have declined (`refusal`), or the text may not match the shape your code needs. Learning Desk treats the first two as errors in `provider.send` and checks the third in validation.

And even a complete, well-formed reply can be factually wrong. Transport success, format validity and correctness are three separate questions.

api-keys-auth.title: API keys and authentication basics
api-keys-auth.summary: How a key proves who is calling, where to keep it, and how to read 401 and 403.
api-keys-auth.objective: Explain how an API key identifies the caller, keep keys out of code, logs and history, and interpret authentication and permission failures.
api-keys-auth.intro: An API key is a long random string that tells the provider which account is calling. Anyone who holds it can make requests, and spend money, as you. Handling keys well is mostly about *where they live*: in the environment, never in source code, logs, exports or screenshots.
keyIdeas: Authentication asks who is calling (401 when it fails); authorisation asks what they may do (403).
An API key is a bearer secret: whoever presents it is treated as you.
Keep keys in the environment and load them at run time; keep them out of git.
HTTPS protects the key in transit. It cannot protect a key you have pasted somewhere else.

sections.title: Who is calling, and what may they do?
sections.body:
Two different questions hide behind "access denied". **Authentication** establishes identity: is this a valid credential? **Authorisation** establishes permission: may this identity use this model or feature? HTTP gives them different statuses. 401 means the request is not authenticated; 403 means the server knows who you are but refuses.

Anthropic's API follows the same split: 401 `authentication_error` for a malformed, revoked or expired key, and 403 `permission_error` when the key lacks permission for the resource.

sections.title: Credentials travel in headers
sections.body: HTTP's general pattern is an `Authorization: <type> <credentials>` header. Model providers document their own header names. Anthropic currently accepts `Authorization: Bearer <key>` or the older `x-api-key` header, alongside a required `anthropic-version` header. Official SDKs add these for you, which is one reason to use them.

sections.title: Keeping keys out of code
sections.body:
Put the key in an **environment variable**. Python reads environment variables through `os.environ`; many projects load a local `.env` file into the environment at start-up with `python-dotenv`. The `.env` file must be listed in `.gitignore` so it never enters version control, where it would persist in history even after deletion.

OWASP's guidance adds operational habits: avoid hard-coding secrets, grant the least privilege needed, and rotate secrets regularly. A per-project key with a spend limit is easier to revoke and limits damage if it leaks.
sections.callout: Search before you commit: a key pasted into a test file is the most common leak.

sections.title: Transport security
sections.body: HTTPS (HTTP over TLS) encrypts the request, headers included, between your computer and the provider. MDN notes that some schemes, such as Basic authentication, only *encode* credentials, so they are insecure without HTTPS. TLS does nothing for a key that appears in a screenshot, a shared log, a chat message or an exported file.

sections.title: Worked example: how Learning Desk handles the key
sections.body: Learning Desk never reads, stores or displays the key's value. `config.api_key_present()` only reports whether one is set, which is what Settings shows. The Anthropic SDK reads `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` from the environment itself. `provider.build_request` builds the request without credentials, so the request saved in every call record contains none. A rejected key becomes a clear 401 message rather than a stack trace.

sections.title: Misconception: a private repository is a safe place for a key
sections.body: Private repositories get cloned to laptops, shared with collaborators, connected to CI services, and occasionally made public. Git history keeps every committed version, so deleting the line later does not remove it. Treat any key that has been committed as leaked: revoke it in the provider console, create a new one, and update your `.env`.

tokens-context-window.title: Tokens and the context window
tokens-context-window.summary: What a model actually reads, what counts toward its limit, and what happens when a request is too long.
tokens-context-window.objective: Explain how text becomes tokens, list everything that counts toward a context window, and predict what happens when a request does not fit.
tokens-context-window.intro: Language models do not read characters or words. They read **tokens**: pieces of text from a fixed vocabulary that the model's tokenizer produces. Limits, prices and speed are all measured in tokens, and every request has a **context window**: the maximum number of tokens the model can take into account at once, including what it writes back.
keyIdeas: A token is a piece of text from the model's vocabulary, often part of a word, often with a leading space.
Counts depend on the tokenizer, so the same text can count differently on different models.
The context window covers instructions, messages, tool definitions and the reply being generated.
More context is not automatically better: it costs time and money and can reduce recall.

sections.title: What a token is
sections.body:
Tokenizers split text into units that balance two needs: a vocabulary small enough to learn and pieces meaningful enough to be useful. Sub-word methods such as byte pair encoding keep common words whole and split rare words into smaller, reusable pieces, so the model can handle words it never saw whole.

Two consequences are easy to miss. Spaces usually belong to the following token, so `" notes"` and `"notes"` can be different tokens. And code, numbers, unusual names and many non-English languages tend to use more tokens per word than everyday English prose.

sections.title: Counting depends on the model
sections.body:
Each model family has its own tokenizer, so token counts are not portable. Anthropic's documentation notes that its newer models use a tokenizer that produces roughly 30% more tokens for the same text than earlier models, and advises recounting prompts for the model you plan to use rather than reusing old counts.

To measure rather than guess, use the provider's token-counting tool (Anthropic offers a free endpoint that returns an estimate), or read the `usage` field every response reports. Learning Desk saves that usage in each call record.
sections.callout: Word counts are a poor proxy for tokens. When you need a length limit in a prompt, sentences or paragraphs work better than an exact word count.

sections.title: What fills the window
sections.body:
Everything in a request counts: the system instructions, every message (including earlier turns, tool results, images and documents), the tool definitions, and the output the model generates for this turn. In a chat, earlier turns are sent again with every new message, so history grows until it dominates.

Window sizes vary by model. At the time of checking, Anthropic listed a 1M-token window for its current models and 200k for some older ones, with up to 128k output tokens per request on the 1M-token models. The same documentation warns that accuracy and recall can degrade as context grows, so curating what goes in matters as much as the limit.

sections.title: When it does not fit
sections.body:
What happens depends on the provider and model. On Anthropic's API, input that alone exceeds the window is rejected with a 400 error ("prompt is too long"). On newer models, a request whose input plus `max_tokens` exceeds the window is accepted, and generation stops with the stop reason `model_context_window_exceeded` if it reaches the limit. Separately, any reply stops with `max_tokens` when it reaches the requested output limit.

Learning Desk guards earlier and more crudely: before any call, a source over 100,000 characters or 500 passages is refused with a message asking for a shorter passage. That is a character limit, not a token count, chosen to keep requests bounded and predictable.

sections.title: Worked example: budgeting a conversation
sections.body: Suppose a chat uses 1,200 tokens of system instructions, each exchange (question plus answer) averages 800 tokens, and you reserve 1,500 tokens for the next reply. Because earlier turns are resent, the request grows with every exchange:
sections.callout: By exchange 40, history is over 90% of the request. Summarising or selecting earlier turns is the usual remedy.

sections.title: Misconception: a token is a word
sections.body: Some words are one token, others several, and punctuation and spaces are part of tokens too. Rules of thumb about characters or words per token are rough averages for one kind of text and one tokenizer. For anything that matters (cost estimates, fitting a document, setting limits) count with the tool for your model or read the reported usage.

context-vs-storage.title: Context versus storage: what a model actually sees
context-vs-storage.summary: Why a stateless API forgets, how apps create memory, and how Learning Desk chooses context.
context-vs-storage.objective: Distinguish the context sent with one request from the data an application stores, and decide deliberately what each request should include.
context-vs-storage.intro: People often say a model "remembers" a conversation. With an API such as Anthropic's Messages API, it does not: each request is processed on its own, and the application sends the conversation again every time. **Storage** is what your application keeps between requests. **Context** is what one request contains. Keeping the two apart explains most "why did it forget?" surprises, and most privacy questions too.
keyIdeas: The Messages API is stateless: the client sends the full history it wants the model to use.
A chat app's "memory" is the application deciding what to resend.
Storage persists between requests; context exists only inside one request.
Choosing context is a design decision with effects on quality, cost and privacy.

sections.title: Stateless requests
sections.body:
Anthropic's documentation states it directly: the Messages API is stateless, so you always send the full conversational history. A multi-turn conversation is just a `messages` list that grows on the client and is sent in full each time. Earlier turns do not even need to have come from the model; an application can supply them.

This is the same property as HTTP's statelessness, one level up: each request stands alone, and continuity is built by what the client chooses to send.
sections.code:
turn_1 = [{"role": "user", "content": "My name is Sam."}]
# … reply: "Nice to meet you, Sam." …

turn_2_alone = [{"role": "user", "content": "What is my name?"}]

turn_2_with_history = [
    {"role": "user", "content": "My name is Sam."},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "Nice to meet you, Sam."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "What is my name?"},
]

sections.title: Storage is the application's job
sections.body:
Anything that should persist (notes, past reviews, settings, logs) has to be stored by the application, for example in a database. Learning Desk uses one SQLite file on your computer for sessions, resources, summaries, quiz attempts and every AI call record.

Storing something does not send it anywhere. A record only reaches a model if code reads it and places it in a request. That is the boundary to look for when you ask "what does the model know?" or "what left my computer?"

sections.title: How Learning Desk builds context
sections.body:
For a notebook review, `ai.prepare_snapshot` reads the **saved** session (title, topic, goal, explanation, notes, sources) and its open queue items, splits the text into numbered sections [S1], [S2], … and stores that snapshot. Identical content reuses the same snapshot row. The request contains the fixed instructions plus that numbered snapshot, nothing else: no other sessions, no earlier reviews, no call logs.

Reader actions follow the same rule with a different source: a summary or quiz sends only the selected content version of one resource. Because snapshots and versions are kept, every saved review, summary and question can be traced back to exactly what the model was shown.

sections.title: Choosing what to include
sections.body:
Every request is a selection problem. Include too little and the model lacks what it needs; include too much and you pay in tokens and time, may reduce recall, and send data that did not need to leave. Common strategies:

- **Scope**: send one session or one document, not everything (Learning Desk's choice).
- **Select**: retrieve the most relevant passages (see the retrieval lesson).
- **Summarise**: replace old turns with a summary; providers increasingly offer server-side compaction for long conversations.
- **Cache**: prompt caching makes a repeated prefix cheaper and faster to process, but the cached tokens are still part of the request and still occupy the window.

sections.title: Worked example: why the review did not mention last week
sections.body:
You review today's session and the feedback ignores a misconception you corrected in last week's session. Walk the boundary:

1. **Is last week in storage?** Yes, as a separate session row.
2. **Is it in context?** No. The snapshot contains only the current session's saved fields and open queue items.
3. **Could the model know anyway?** Not from your data; it only sees the request.
4. **Fix, if you want it considered**: add a short note or source line to *this* session, save, and review again. You then control exactly what is shared.

sections.title: Misconception: the provider remembers my earlier requests
sections.body: Whatever a provider retains under its data policies, the model's reply to a request is produced from that request's context (and what the model learned in training), not from your earlier API calls. If an application seems to remember, it is resending or retrieving earlier material. Prompt caching does not change this: it reuses processing of a prefix you send again, and the cached tokens still count as part of the request's context.

sampling-temperature.title: Next-token probabilities and sampling
sampling-temperature.summary: How a model turns scores into probabilities, and how temperature, top-k and top-p change the choice.
sampling-temperature.objective: Explain how a language model turns scores into a probability distribution over next tokens, and predict how temperature, top-k and top-p change which token is chosen.
sampling-temperature.intro: A language model generates text one token at a time. At each step it produces a score for every token in its vocabulary, those scores become probabilities, and a **decoding** rule picks one token. The chosen token is appended and the process repeats. Sampling settings change only that last step, but because every choice becomes context for the next, small changes can lead to very different text.
keyIdeas: At each step the model scores every token; softmax turns the scores into probabilities that sum to 1.
Generation is a loop: choose a token, append it, score again.
Temperature reshapes the whole distribution; top-k and top-p remove the unlikely tail.
Which controls you can set is provider- and model-specific. Check before relying on them.

sections.title: From scores to probabilities
sections.body:
The model's raw scores (often called logits) can be any real numbers. **Softmax** converts them into probabilities: raise *e* to each score, then divide by the total so everything sums to 1. Higher scores get exponentially more probability. With temperature *T*, each score is divided by *T* first:

p(token i) = exp(s_i / T) / Σ exp(s_j / T)

The interactive chart uses eight invented candidate words for the prompt *"The experiment finished, so we wrote the …"*. A real model would score its entire vocabulary, often tens of thousands of tokens.

sections.title: One token at a time
sections.body:
Generation repeats a simple loop: score, choose, append. The choice at step 1 becomes part of the context for step 2, so a less likely early token can lead to a different sentence, paragraph or argument. This is why two runs with the same prompt can diverge widely even when each individual choice looked similar.

The loop stops when the model produces an end-of-turn token, a stop sequence appears, or the output reaches `max_tokens`: the `stop_reason` in a response tells you which.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.body:
Dividing scores by *T* below 1 stretches the differences between them: the top candidate gains probability and the tail shrinks. *T* above 1 compresses the differences: the distribution flattens and unlikely tokens are chosen more often. As *T* approaches 0, sampling approaches **greedy decoding**, always taking the single most likely token.

Temperature never changes the *ranking* of candidates, only how much the ranking matters.

sections.title: Top-k and top-p
sections.body:
**Top-k** keeps only the *k* most likely tokens and renormalises. **Top-p** (nucleus sampling) keeps the smallest set of most likely tokens whose probabilities add up to at least *p*, so the number kept adapts to how confident the model is. Holtzman and colleagues proposed nucleus sampling because sampling from the full distribution lets the unreliable low-probability tail produce incoherent text, while always taking the most likely tokens tends to produce bland, repetitive text.

Samplers commonly apply temperature first and then truncation; the chart here does the same.

sections.title: What you can actually control
sections.body:
Exposed settings differ by provider and model, and change over time. At the time of checking, Anthropic's documentation said `temperature`, `top_p` and `top_k` are **not supported** on its Claude 4.7 and later models (or on any model from API version 2026-10-21): setting them returns a 400 error, and the guidance is to steer behaviour with prompting instead. Learning Desk sends none of these parameters.

Whatever your provider allows, the robust practices are the same: constrain the *format* with structured outputs, cache results you want to stay stable, and evaluate across several runs rather than trusting one.
sections.callout: This lesson teaches the general mechanism. Do not assume any particular provider lets you set these values.

sections.title: Worked example: one distribution, five settings
sections.body: The table applies five settings to the same invented scores. Read across a row to see one candidate's fate. Notice that lower temperature concentrates probability on *report*, higher temperature lifts *poem* and *banana*, and both truncation methods remove the tail entirely while boosting what remains.

sections.title: Misconception: low temperature makes answers correct
sections.body: Greedy or low-temperature decoding picks the *most likely* continuation, and likely is not the same as true. A model that assigns high probability to a wrong statement will state it more consistently, not less. Lower randomness also does not, by itself, promise identical output on every run; do not assume that unless your provider documents it. Correctness has to be checked by evaluation, not dialled in.

activity.title: Predict, then move the sliders
steps: Before touching anything, predict: at temperature 0.2, roughly what share will *report* get?
Set temperature to 0.2 and check. Then try 2.0. What happens to *banana*?
Return to 1.0. Set top-k to 2. Which candidates survive, and why do their shares go up?
Set top-k back to 0 (off) and top-p to 0.5. How many candidates are kept?
Draw three samples at two different temperatures and compare how often each word appears.

checks.prompt: Raising temperature from 1.0 to 2.0 does what to the distribution?
options: Flattens it, so less likely tokens are chosen more often
Sharpens it toward the top token
Removes all but the top two tokens
checks.answer: Flattens it, so less likely tokens are chosen more often
checks.explanation: Dividing scores by a larger T shrinks their differences.

Tokens with at least 90% probability each
checks.answer: The smallest set of most likely tokens whose probabilities reach 90%
checks.explanation: Nucleus sampling keeps a variable-size set covering probability mass p.

options: No. It changes how strongly the ranking is followed
checks.answer: No. It changes how strongly the ranking is followed
checks.explanation: Temperature rescales all scores by the same factor, so order is preserved.

attention-basics.title: Attention: how tokens use other tokens
attention-basics.summary: What an attention weight means, how to read an attention pattern, and where attention fits in a transformer.
attention-basics.objective: Describe what an attention weight represents, compute one attention step on tiny numbers, and read an attention pattern without over-interpreting it.
attention-basics.intro: Inside a transformer, each token is represented by a vector. On its own, the vector for *it* in "the animal didn't cross the street because it was tired" cannot say what *it* refers to. **Attention** is the operation that lets each token gather information from other tokens' vectors, weighting some much more than others. Stacked many times, it is the core of the transformer architecture.
keyIdeas: Attention lets each token build a new vector as a weighted mix of other tokens' information.
For one token, the weights are non-negative and sum to 1: a probability distribution.
Queries and keys decide the weights; values are what gets mixed.
In text generators, a causal mask stops tokens from looking at later tokens.
Models use many heads and layers; one heatmap is a narrow view.

sections.title: Why attention
sections.body: Earlier neural translation systems squeezed a whole source sentence into one fixed-length vector before producing the translation. Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio (2014) let the model instead *softly search* the source for the positions relevant to each word it produced, a learned alignment. Vaswani and colleagues (2017) went further: the Transformer drops recurrence and convolutions and is built from attention (plus simple feed-forward layers), which also made training more parallel.

sections.title: Queries, keys and values
sections.body:
Each token's vector is projected three ways. A **query** describes what this token is looking for; a **key** describes what each token offers; a **value** is the information each token contributes if chosen. The weight between two tokens comes from how well the query matches the key (a dot product), scaled by the square root of the key dimension and passed through softmax. The output is the weighted sum of values:

Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q·Kᵀ / √d_k) · V

Softmax is the same function as in the sampling lesson, used here to turn match scores into weights rather than to choose a word.

sections.title: Reading an attention heatmap
sections.body:
In a heatmap, each **row** is a token being updated and each **column** a token it can draw from; each row sums to 1. Generative language models use a **causal mask**: a token may attend to itself and earlier tokens only, because later tokens do not exist yet when it is generated. That leaves the upper-right triangle empty.

In the illustrative head here, the row for *it* puts most of its weight on *animal*: the kind of pattern that would help resolve the pronoun. Real heads learn their patterns during training; some are interpretable like this, many are not.

sections.title: Heads, layers and position
sections.body:
A transformer runs several attention **heads** in parallel, each with its own projections, so different heads can track different relationships. Their outputs are combined and passed through a feed-forward layer, and this block is repeated across many **layers**, each refining every token's vector.

Attention by itself has no notion of order: it compares vectors regardless of where they sit. The original Transformer therefore added positional encodings to the token vectors. How position is represented is an active design choice in later models.

sections.title: Worked example: one attention step with tiny numbers
sections.body:
Take three tokens with two-dimensional keys and values, and the query of the third token q = (1.0, 0.5). The keys are k₁ = (1, 0), k₂ = (0, 1), k₃ = (1, 1); the values are v₁ = (1, 0), v₂ = (0, 1), v₃ = (0.5, 0.5).

1. **Scores** = q·k / √2: 0.707, 0.354, 1.061.
2. **Softmax** turns them into weights: 0.320, 0.225, 0.456 (they sum to 1).
3. **Mix the values**: 0.320·v₁ + 0.225·v₂ + 0.456·v₃ = (0.548, 0.452).

The third token's new vector leans toward the tokens whose keys best matched its query. That is all one head does; the model learns the projections that make useful matches.

sections.title: Misconception: attention weights explain the answer
sections.body: A heatmap shows how one head in one layer mixed information for one input. The model has many heads and layers, feed-forward computation between them, and the final output depends on all of it. Attention patterns can suggest hypotheses about what a model uses, but treating a single map as *the reason* for an output over-reads it. The heatmap in this lesson is invented to illustrate the mechanism, not taken from a real model.

steps: Use the explorer below. Choose the row for *it* and read its three largest weights.

Choose *The* (the first token). Why can it only attend to itself?

checks.explanation: Weights are softmax(Q·Kᵀ/√d_k); values are then mixed using those weights.

embeddings-similarity.title: Embeddings and similarity
embeddings-similarity.summary: What an embedding vector represents, how cosine similarity compares two of them, and what a score can't tell you.
embeddings-similarity.objective: Explain what an embedding represents, compute cosine similarity for small vectors, and recognise what a similarity score can and cannot tell you.
embeddings-similarity.intro: An **embedding** is a list of numbers that an embedding model produces for a piece of text. The model is trained so that texts with related meaning get vectors pointing in similar directions. That turns a fuzzy question ("which of my notes is about this?") into arithmetic you can do quickly over thousands of passages, which is the basis of semantic search and retrieval.
keyIdeas: An embedding model maps text to a fixed-length vector of numbers.
Related meanings tend to produce vectors that point in similar directions.
Cosine similarity compares direction; for unit-length vectors it equals the dot product.
Similar is not the same as relevant, and neither is the same as true.

sections.title: Text as vectors
sections.body:
Mikolov and colleagues (2013) showed that continuous vector representations of words, learned from large text collections, capture syntactic and semantic relationships well enough to score on word-similarity tests. Modern embedding models apply the same idea to whole sentences and passages, producing one vector per input.

The vectors are long. Anthropic, for example, does not offer its own embedding model and points to Voyage AI, whose current general-purpose models return 1,024 numbers by default (with 256, 512 or 2,048 as options). Each number has no meaning on its own; meaning lives in the relationships between whole vectors.

sections.title: Measuring similarity
sections.body:
**Cosine similarity** measures the angle between two vectors: 1 means the same direction, 0 means perpendicular (unrelated in this sense), and −1 means opposite. It is the dot product divided by the product of the lengths, so it ignores how long the vectors are.

Many embedding models return unit-length (normalised) vectors. Then the lengths are 1, cosine similarity equals the dot product, and ranking by Euclidean distance gives the same order. Check your model's documentation before relying on that.
sections.code:
import math

def cosine(a, b):
    dot = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    length = math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in a)) * math.sqrt(sum(y * y for y in b))
    return dot / length

cosine([1, 2, 0], [2, 4, 1])   # 0.976: nearly the same direction
cosine([1, 2, 0], [-2, 1, 0])  # 0.0: perpendicular

sections.title: A picture you should not over-read
sections.body: The map places nine phrases by hand in two dimensions so that angles from the origin mirror meaning: animals one way, payments another, code a third. It is useful for building intuition about direction and nearest neighbours, and misleading if taken literally. Real embeddings have hundreds or thousands of dimensions, and any flattening of them to two dimensions distorts distances.
sections.callout: Toy data. Use it to see the idea of 'nearest by angle', not to judge how a real model would place these phrases.

sections.title: Queries and documents
sections.body: In search, a short question and a long passage are different kinds of text. Some embedding providers therefore distinguish them: Voyage's documentation recommends setting `input_type` to `query` or `document`, which prepends a different instruction before embedding and can improve retrieval quality. Whatever the provider, embed your documents once, store the vectors, and embed each new query at search time with the same model. Vectors from different models are not comparable.

sections.title: Worked example: cosine similarity by hand
sections.body:
Compare a = (1, 2, 0) with b = (2, 4, 1) and c = (−2, 1, 0).

1. **a·b** = 1×2 + 2×4 + 0×1 = 10. Lengths: |a| = √5 ≈ 2.236, |b| = √21 ≈ 4.583. Cosine = 10 / (2.236 × 4.583) ≈ **0.976**.
2. **a·c** = 1×(−2) + 2×1 + 0×0 = 0, so the cosine is **0**: the vectors are perpendicular.

b is almost a scaled copy of a (twice as long, with a small extra component), so its direction barely differs. Length did not matter, only direction.

sections.title: Misconception: a high score means the passage answers the question
sections.body: Embeddings capture overall relatedness. A passage can be strongly about the same topic as a question without answering it, and two sentences that differ by a single *not* are about the same subject, so they may score as similar while meaning opposite things. Treat similarity as a way to *shortlist* candidates. Whether a passage actually answers the question, and whether it is correct, needs reading, a reranker, or evaluation.

retrieval-basics.title: Retrieval: choose documents before generating
retrieval-basics.summary: Separate selecting material from writing an answer, and diagnose which stage went wrong.
retrieval-basics.objective: Separate retrieval (selecting material) from generation (writing an answer), and diagnose which stage caused a poor answer.
retrieval-basics.intro: You cannot send everything you have with every request, and you should not: it costs tokens, time and privacy, and can reduce quality. **Retrieval** selects a few relevant passages first; **generation** then writes an answer using only those. The combination is usually called retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Treating the two stages separately is the key to building and debugging it.
keyIdeas: RAG pairs a retriever that selects passages with a generator that writes from them.
The model can only use what retrieval puts into its context.
Chunking decides what can be found; chunks can lose the context that made them findable.
Evaluate retrieval and generation separately; they fail in different ways.

sections.title: Two stages
sections.body: Lewis and colleagues (2020) combined a pre-trained generator (knowledge stored in its weights, *parametric* memory) with a dense vector index of Wikipedia searched by a neural retriever (*non-parametric* memory). The pattern generalises: an index you control supplies material at request time, so answers can draw on documents the model never saw in training, and you can update the documents without retraining anything.

sections.title: Indexing: chunks and vectors
sections.body:
Before searching, documents are split into **chunks**, each chunk is embedded, and the vectors are stored with a pointer back to the text. Chunk size is a trade-off: small chunks match precisely but may lack context; large chunks keep context but dilute the match and cost more tokens when included.

Learning Desk splits text in a related way for a different purpose: `sections.split_blocks` breaks a source on blank lines, never inside a fenced code block, and numbers the passages so the model can cite them. The app does not embed or search them; the whole selected version is sent. That works because sources are short and bounded.

sections.title: Selecting: similarity and beyond
sections.body: The simplest retriever embeds the question and takes the *k* chunks with the highest cosine similarity. Anthropic's write-up on contextual retrieval describes common improvements: combine embeddings with keyword search (BM25) because exact terms such as names and error codes matter, merge the two rankings, and rerank the candidates with a model to keep only the most relevant. The same write-up names a core weakness of chunking: a chunk such as "revenue grew by 3%" can lose the company and period it referred to, so it is never retrieved. Adding brief document context to each chunk before indexing addresses that.

sections.title: Generating with citations
sections.body: The generator receives instructions, the selected chunks (numbered), and the question, and is asked to answer from them and cite chunk numbers. Citations make answers checkable, but a citation check has limits. Learning Desk's `check_refs` rejects replies whose references do not resolve to a supplied passage; the app's own documentation is explicit that this establishes that a passage *exists*, not that it *supports* the claim.
sections.callout: Existence of a citation is cheap to verify in code. Support needs reading or a separate grader.

sections.title: Worked example: diagnosing a wrong answer
sections.body: A user asks "How long are summaries cached?" and gets a wrong answer. Work stage by stage:

rows: Is the correct passage in the index at all?
Is it among the top k for this question?
Add keyword search, rerank, add chunk context, raise k
Does the answer follow from the passages it was given?
The model misread or added claims
Tighten instructions; require quotes; grade support
Do the citations point at the passages actually used?
Validate citations; show passages beside claims

sections.title: Misconception: retrieval stops hallucination
sections.body: Retrieval gives the model better material; it does not force the model to use it faithfully. The generator can still misread a passage, merge two passages incorrectly, or add plausible claims that appear in neither. And if retrieval selected the wrong passages, a faithful answer will be faithfully wrong. RAG reduces some failure modes and introduces others, which is why both stages need their own evaluation.

activity.title: Be the retriever
steps: Question: "Why does the app refuse very long sources?" Read these five chunks:

(1) Summaries are cached per version and format. (2) Imports reject private network addresses. (3) Sources over 100,000 characters or 500 passages are refused before any call. (4) Each request uses one call; no automatic retry. (5) Long requests cost more tokens and time.
Choose the two chunks you would send. Which words did you match on, and which did you infer?
Which chunk would a keyword search find most easily? Which needs meaning rather than words?
Write the one-sentence answer, citing your chunks. Would it still be right if you had picked (1) and (4)?

checks.prompt: The correct passage exists in the index but was not in the top 5. Which stage failed?
checks.answer: Retrieval
checks.explanation: The model never received the passage, so generation could not use it.

checks.prompt: What does Learning Desk's citation check establish?
options: That each cited passage exists in the supplied source
That each claim is supported by its passage
checks.answer: That each cited passage exists in the supplied source
checks.explanation: The check resolves references; it does not judge support or truth.

To make chunks longer for the model
To reduce the number of chunks

checks.explanation: Contextual retrieval restores the missing context so the chunk matches relevant questions.

structured-outputs.title: Structured outputs: schemas and validation
structured-outputs.summary: Ask for a machine-readable shape, verify what comes back, and handle the replies that fail.
structured-outputs.objective: Request machine-readable replies with a schema, validate them in code, and design what happens when validation fails.
structured-outputs.intro: An application cannot store "a nice paragraph"; it needs fields: a takeaway, a list of citations, a question with four options and one key. **Structured output** means asking the model for a specific JSON shape and then **validating** what comes back before anything is saved. The two steps are separate, and both matter.
keyIdeas: Asking for a shape (a schema) and checking it (validation) are separate steps.
Constrained decoding can make replies schema-compliant, with documented exceptions.
Some rules cannot be expressed in a provider schema; enforce them in your own code.
A rejected reply should be logged and surfaced, never silently patched.

sections.title: Why structure
sections.body: Free text is for people; fields are for programs. With fields, the interface can place the takeaway beside its citations, the database can store each question separately, and code can check rules such as "the key is one of the options". Structure also makes failures visible: a missing field is detectable, a vague paragraph is not.

sections.title: Asking for a shape
sections.body:
Anthropic's API accepts a JSON Schema in `output_config.format` with type `json_schema`, and uses constrained decoding so the reply's text is schema-compliant JSON. Learning Desk's `provider.build_request` does exactly this for every AI action.

Provider schemas support a subset of JSON Schema. At the time of checking, unsupported features included string length limits (`minLength`, `maxLength`), numeric limits (`minimum`, `maximum`), and array limits beyond `minItems` of 0 or 1; using them returns a 400 error. Learning Desk's `learning.schema()` therefore removes those keywords from the schema it sends and enforces the same limits locally with Pydantic.

sections.title: Validating in code
sections.body:
Validation turns "probably the right shape" into "checked". Pydantic models describe the expected fields and types; `model_validate` (or `model_validate_json`) raises a `ValidationError` listing every problem when data does not fit.

In Learning Desk, `ai._run` parses the reply with `json.loads`, validates it with the action's Pydantic model, then runs any extra rules. If anything fails, the call is recorded as an error with the raw reply and the message "did not match the expected format", and your notes are untouched.

sections.title: Rules a schema cannot express
sections.body:
Some requirements depend on relationships between fields or on data outside the reply:

- A multiple-choice key must equal one of four *distinct* options (`PracticeQuestion` checks this).
- A quick read must leave the explanation and example fields empty.
- Every citation must refer to a passage that was actually supplied (`check_refs`).

These belong in code after schema validation. Keep each rule small and give it a specific error message, so a failure points to the exact rule that was broken.

sections.title: Worked example: a validator for quiz questions
sections.body: This is a shortened version of the model Learning Desk uses for generated questions. Field types and lengths are declared; the cross-field rule lives in a validator that runs after the fields are parsed.

sections.title: Misconception: with structured outputs, validation is unnecessary
sections.body: Anthropic's own documentation lists cases where output may not match the schema: a refusal (`stop_reason: "refusal"`), a reply cut off at the token limit (`max_tokens`), and enum or const values that differ only in capitalisation. Add the constraints you had to remove from the provider schema, and the rules no schema can express, and local validation is still essential. It is also what keeps your application safe if you change provider or model.

tools-agent-loop.title: Tools and the agent loop
tools-agent-loop.summary: How a model requests a tool, who runs it, and how to keep a loop of tool calls bounded.
tools-agent-loop.objective: Explain how a model requests tool calls, who executes them, and how to bound an agent loop with checks, budgets and stop conditions.
tools-agent-loop.intro: A model on its own can only produce text. **Tools** let it ask an application to do something: search, read a file, call an API. The model proposes a structured call; for tools you define, **your code** runs it and sends back the result. Repeat that in a loop and you have an **agent**. The engineering is mostly about the loop's edges: what may run, with which inputs, and when to stop.
keyIdeas: A tool definition has a name, a description and an input schema.
The model returns a tool_use request; your application runs client tools and returns a tool_result.
A workflow follows predefined code paths; an agent lets the model direct its own steps.
Start simple. Add permission checks, budgets and stop conditions before autonomy.

sections.title: Defining a tool
sections.body: A tool is described to the model, not given to it. The **name** identifies it, the **description** says when and why to use it (the model relies heavily on this), and the **input schema** is a JSON Schema for its arguments. Tool definitions are sent with the request, so they count as input tokens.

sections.title: The round trip
sections.body:
When the model decides to use a client tool, the response ends with `stop_reason: "tool_use"` and contains a `tool_use` block with an id, the tool name and its input. Your code runs the operation and sends a new request that includes the earlier turns plus a `tool_result` block carrying the same id and the output. The model then continues: it may answer, or ask for another tool.

Anthropic also offers **server tools** (such as web search) that run on its infrastructure; you see their results without executing anything. For your own tools, execution and its consequences are always your application's responsibility.

sections.title: From one call to a loop
sections.body:
Anthropic's *Building effective agents* distinguishes **workflows**, where models and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths, from **agents**, where the model directs its own process and tool use. The ReAct paper showed the value of interleaving reasoning with actions: the reasoning chooses the next action, and the action's result informs the reasoning.

Each iteration resends the growing conversation, so long loops cost more per step, and an early mistake can compound.

sections.title: Bounding the loop
sections.body:
The same article recommends finding the simplest solution that works, often a single well-prepared call, and adding agentic complexity only when it pays off. When you do build a loop, design its edges:

- **Allowlist** the tools; reject any other name.
- **Validate inputs** against the schema and your own rules before running anything.
- **Confirm consequential actions** (sending, deleting, paying) with a person.
- **Budget** steps, tokens and time, and stop when any runs out.
- **Test in a sandbox** before giving access to anything real.
sections.callout: Tool results are untrusted input too: a fetched web page can contain instructions aimed at the model.

sections.title: Worked example: a bounded loop
sections.body: A sketch of the control flow, with the provider call and tools passed in as functions. It is illustrative pseudocode in Python syntax; the app does not run it.

sections.title: Misconception: the model runs the tool
sections.body: For client tools the model only *proposes* a call: a name and some arguments in JSON. Your code decides whether to run it, with what checks, and what to report back. That is good news: every safety measure (allowlists, validation, confirmation, sandboxing) lives in code you control. It also means you cannot blame the model for an action your application chose to execute.

evaluation-basics.title: Evaluation: test cases, graders and failure analysis
evaluation-basics.summary: Build a small fixed test set, pick a grader per criterion, and turn failures into specific fixes.
evaluation-basics.objective: Build a small evaluation set, choose a grading method for each criterion, and turn failures into specific, testable fixes.
evaluation-basics.intro: Trying a prompt a few times and liking the result is not evidence that it works. An **evaluation** runs a fixed set of cases through the system the same way every time and judges each output by a stated standard. It turns "seems better" into "passes 18 of 20, up from 14, and here are the two that still fail".
keyIdeas: An eval is a fixed set of cases run the same way, so results are comparable across changes.
Each case needs an input and a way to judge the output: an expected answer, a rule, or a rubric.
Graders: code (fast, exact), a model with a rubric (nuanced, can be wrong), a person (best, slow).
Read failures, group them by cause, fix the largest group, rerun the same cases.

sections.title: Why a fixed set
sections.body: Models produce varied outputs, and people remember striking examples. A fixed set protects against both: the same inputs, the same grader, a number you can compare. Anthropic's guidance on building evaluations stresses two things that are easy to skip: mirror real usage, **including edge cases** (irrelevant, very long, ambiguous or harmful inputs), and prefer more automatically graded cases with slightly lower signal over a handful of hand-graded ones.

sections.title: Writing test cases
sections.body: A case is an input plus what good looks like. Tag each case with what it is testing so failures can be grouped later. For Learning Desk's *Quick read* (summarise only the supplied source, about 150 words, with citations), a starter set might look like this:

rows: Summary cites passages; no added facts
Short summary; says the source is brief
A tutorial that is mostly code
Describes the code's purpose; cites code passages
Treats it as text to summarise
Summary is faithful; language choice consistent

sections.title: Choosing a grader
sections.body:
Pick the cheapest grader that can actually judge the criterion. Exact rules (valid JSON, required fields, citations resolve, length within bounds) belong in code. Qualities such as faithfulness or tone need a rubric applied by a model or a person.

Model graders are useful but have known biases. Zheng and colleagues found position bias (favouring an answer because of where it appears), verbosity bias (favouring longer answers) and self-enhancement bias (favouring outputs like their own). Anthropic's guidance suggests using a different model as the grader from the one that produced the output, and clear rubrics with a reason before the verdict.

rows: Format, fields, exact answers, citation existence
Biases; extra calls; can be wrong
Ground truth for hard judgements; checking other graders

sections.title: From failures to fixes
sections.body:
A score tells you *how much*; reading failures tells you *why*. For each failing case, write a one-line cause ("added a fact not in the source", "ignored the code block"), then group causes and count. Fix the largest group first, rerun **all** cases (a fix can break something else), and keep the outputs and grader reasons from each run so you can compare.

Keep some cases aside that you do not look at while tuning, so you can tell whether you improved the system or just fitted the test set.

sections.title: Worked example: grading the grader in this app
sections.body:
Learning Desk grades generated multiple-choice questions deterministically: your choice is compared with the saved answer key. That comparison is exact and free, but the key itself was generated by a model, so the grader inherits its errors. The app says so in its feedback: "Matches the saved AI-generated key. The key can itself be wrong."

The *This question or feedback seems wrong* report is the failure-analysis loop in miniature: it saves the question, attempt and feedback ids so a suspect key can be examined later, without another model call.

rows: Key is one of four distinct options
Agreement with the key, not proven correctness
A model's judgement, with stated uncertainty

sections.title: Misconception: a high score means the system is good
sections.body: A score is only as meaningful as its cases and its grader. Twenty easy cases graded leniently can score 100% on a system that fails real users. Before trusting a number, ask: do the cases include the hard and adversarial inputs real use will bring? Has the grader been checked against human judgement on a sample? Did the score move because the system improved, or because the cases or grader changed?

latency-cost-reliability.title: Usefulness, latency, cost and reliability
latency-cost-reliability.summary: Estimate where time and money go in a request, and trade them off deliberately.
latency-cost-reliability.objective: Estimate where time and money go in an AI request, and choose design changes that trade usefulness, latency, cost and reliability deliberately.
latency-cost-reliability.intro: An AI feature succeeds only if it is useful, responds fast enough, costs an acceptable amount, and behaves predictably when things go wrong. These pull against each other: a longer, more careful answer is slower and dearer; automatic retries improve success rates and add cost. Good product decisions make those trade-offs explicit.
keyIdeas: Start from usefulness; a fast, cheap wrong answer has no value.
Output length usually dominates response time; input size matters too.
Price is per token, and output tokens cost more than input tokens on current price lists.
Plan for rate limits, timeouts and invalid replies before they happen.

sections.title: Usefulness first
sections.body: Anthropic's latency guide makes the order explicit: first engineer a prompt that works well without constraints, then try latency reductions, because optimising too early can stop you discovering what good looks like. In practice: define the job, build an evaluation, reach acceptable quality, *then* shorten, cache, stream or switch models, re-running the evaluation after each change.

sections.title: Where time goes
sections.body:
Two measures matter. **Time to first token** (TTFT) is how long until the first piece of output arrives; it shapes how responsive streaming feels. Total time is how long until the reply is complete. Reading the input is relatively fast per token; generating output happens one token at a time, so long outputs dominate.

Levers, in rough order of impact: ask for shorter output and set `max_tokens`, send less input, choose a faster model or lower effort setting, cache repeated prefixes, and stream so people see progress.
sections.callout: The timeline uses invented round-number rates to show proportions. Measure your own requests.

sections.title: Where money goes
sections.body:
Providers price input and output tokens separately, per million tokens. On Anthropic's current price list output costs several times more than input for every model, so verbose replies are expensive twice: in time and in money. Two discounts change the arithmetic: prompt-cache reads are billed at a fraction of the base input price (0.1× on most models at the time of checking), and the Message Batches API offers a 50% reduction for work that can wait.

Do not copy prices into code or notes. They change; read the provider's page and plug current numbers into a calculator like the one in *Try it*.

sections.title: Reliability
sections.body:
Plan for each failure the request flow can produce. Rate limits are measured per minute in requests, input tokens and output tokens; exceeding one returns 429, often with a `retry-after` header saying how long to wait. Overload, timeouts and invalid replies need their own handling, and every retry costs another request.

Learning Desk's choices, for comparison: one attempt per click; a configurable timeout (`LEARNING_DESK_TIMEOUT`, 180 seconds by default); validation before saving; and summaries cached per content version, so opening a saved summary again costs nothing and takes no time.

sections.title: Misconception: streaming makes requests faster
sections.body: Streaming sends tokens as they are generated, so people can start reading after the time to first token. The model still generates the same number of tokens at the same pace, so the total time is essentially unchanged. Streaming improves *perceived* responsiveness, and is worth having for that reason, but it does not reduce cost or total latency.
